title: Foreseen, yet free (Avot 3:15)
hookLine: all is foreseen, yet freedom is given, and the world is judged with goodness
tomorrow: who's keeping the record, and what's written in it?

cards: On a stage floor there are little marks of colored tape. The director put them down weeks ago: you'll stand here, then here. Every actor's feet are foreseen.

And still, how you cross from one mark to the next, fast, slow, afraid, laughing, is yours. Akiva's line would fit on one of those strips: hakol tzafui, veharshut netunah. All is foreseen, and permission is given.

teach.b: Akiva doesn't explain how both can be true. He sets them side by side with an and between them. Tzafui means seen ahead, watched.
Reshut means permission, room, freedom to act. Later thinkers worked hard at the knot.
Maimonides calls free choice a pillar of the Torah, and says that God's knowing isn't like ours, so we can't picture how it fits with our choosing. Others simply hold both and keep walking.
And notice how big and how small the words are. Hakol, all: not some, not only the big moments. Reshut, permission, is given: a gift, not something grabbed.
Then Akiva adds two more phrases.
The world is judged with goodness, uvetov ha'olam nidon. And all according to the weight of deeds. That isn't a trap.
It's a promise: the judging leans kind, and it looks at the whole of a life, not one bad night.
So the free part is real, and it adds up. Every step between the tape marks counts.

how: Jews study Avot 3:15 together with Maimonides' laws of repentance, chapter five, where free choice is called a pillar of the Torah.

o: decided in advance, so choices change nothing
seen ahead by God, while freedom is still given
hidden from people until the end of days

games.q: Akiva's two halves — tap the pairs.

s: Akiva explains exactly how foreknowledge and freedom fit together
he sets them side by side and leaves the how open.
Maimonides calls free choice a pillar of the Torah
in his laws of repentance, chapter five.
Akiva's line says the world is judged harshly
uvetov ha'olam nidon: the world is judged with goodness.

games.q: you didn't get the job you wanted, and your aunt says, "it was meant to be." by Akiva's line, what's true?
o: both: it may be foreseen, and what you do next is still free.
nothing you do now matters; it was all decided.
she's wrong; nothing is ever foreseen at all.
games.why: Akiva sets them side by side: all is foreseen, and permission is given. He doesn't let either cancel the other.

practice: Sit with both feet flat and feel exactly where they are, the mark you're on. Choose one small movement, a hand turning over, a slow shift of weight, and before you make it, notice that it hasn't happened yet.
Then make it, slowly, and feel that it was yours.

wordCard.voice: Foreseen. Tzafui in Akiva's Hebrew: seen ahead, and in the very same line, freedom given.

orig.note: Hebrew: permission is given, Akiva's half-line on freedom.

carryVoice: Here's the line: foreseen, yet free, and every step between the marks is yours. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Teshuvah 5:3 and 5:5
